title: Iran War Fallout and Hungary's Pivotal Election
transcriptText:
Hi, I'm Max Bergman.
>> [music]
>> And I'm Donatienne Rouy. And this is The
Euro File, a podcast where we look at
Europe through a Washington lens.
Welcome to another episode of The Euro
File. This week, we're tracking the
continued fallout from the war in Iran,
which has strained Europe's energy
security, its relationship with the
United States, and the future of NATO
itself. Then, we'll turn to a
conversation with Federico Steinberg,
Prince of Asturias Chair at Georgetown
University and Visiting Fellow here at
CSIS, on the war's economic cost for
Europe. Let's get into it. Max, there's
still a lot going on because of
everything happening in Iran, but in
Europe, a lot of jitters are now coming
up because of the energy security issue
in particular.
Can you walk us through the dynamics
that we're seeing? Yeah, we should say
that we're recording on April 7th at
10:21 a.m. Eastern Time. Donald Trump
has basically threatened Iran with
civilizational eraser. Not Europe this
time, but Iran, threatening to bomb
power plants and other infrastructure.
And I think the question is that if he
follows through with that, I mean, that
would sort of amount to a war crime, or
not sort of, it would amount to a war
crime. But, I think the concern in
Europe would also be that the war is
definitely going to be prolonged, but
also a potential for massive civilian
impacts, refugee crisis impacting
Europe. And so, you know, this war is
already being brought home. We are
seeing Dan Jorgensen, the EU Energy
Commissioner from the great country of
Denmark, from where our producer Otto
hails from, basically warning this week
that prices are not going to return to
normal, and that Europe needs to start
preparing for the long haul. We've also
seen a warning from the Economy
Commissioner noting that Europe doesn't
have the same fiscal space as it had
before the last energy crisis. And so,
the same sort of subsidy regimes that
were put in place after the energy
crisis in 2022 might not be applicable.
But, we are seeing things like in Italy
where there's basically a gas tax
holiday being put in place until May.
Spain is doing something similar, trying
reduce the impacts on consumers. And I
think on the one hand, this sort of
short-termism makes sense. Like, you
know, this is an abrupt energy crisis.
On the other hand, this is not going to
end anytime soon. So, if you're doing a
gas tax holiday, and you're not, you
know, working to sort of crush demand or
reduce demand, you're basically just
creating, you know, major budgetary
effects and not facilitating the kind of
transition that would reduce inflation.
And transition doesn't just mean to, you
know, buy EVs, but encouraging people to
drive less and other things.
I guess what I would say here, the basic
hot take takeaway from my view is that I
think Europeans have been slow to
realize that this is an epic crisis. And
therefore,
they need measures not just about gas
tax holidays for a couple months, but
need to start thinking in sort of much
bigger terms in next gen EU style
approaches. The next generation EU was
done in response to COVID to prevent
sort of an economic crisis in Southern
Europe effectively. Now, there's
questions about how impactful that was,
but I think big joint approaches are
needed. For example, Federico Steinberg
and I wrote a piece uh for CSIS calling
for bigger approaches. But, if you look
at a country like Bulgaria, you know,
70% of the vehicles on the road are over
15 years old, right? They're older cars,
they're all gas-powered cars. Bulgaria
also has one of the lowest EV adoption
rates. And you have a German car
industry that is really struggling. One
of the things that we did here in the US
after the Great Financial Crisis was
there was a cash for clunkers deal where
you could trade in your car, you could
get a new one. That was to spur, help
survive the Detroit car sector.
You could see creative approaches like
that. It has to work differently,
obviously, in the EU because you EU
can't go direct to consumers.
But, there is, I think, a need for big,
bold policy approaches that have a very
long-term approach to avoid the kind of
short-termism
of just trying to struggle through this
crisis if it's going to end very soon. I
think we're looking at, at least the
energy analysts, you know, really high
energy prices for the next year at the
very least, and potentially for much
longer. One thing, if we go back to the
2022 energy crisis,
was the speed at which Germany operated.
Like, Germany did not have an ability to
import LNG
prior to the war. And then suddenly, gas
was being cut off. Germany, in a matter
of weeks, figured out ways to import
LNG. And I think a similar approach is
needed now regarding this energy crisis.
How can you reduce gas demand? How can
you reduce oil demand? Are there quick
fixes? Is there enough inventory to
change over, you know, cab fleets from
gas-powered cars to EVs? Anything that
can sort of reduce demand, because if
you're reducing your oil consumption,
you are reducing inflation. And I think
the the danger, as Federico pointed out
in this piece, is that, you know, what
happens is that inflation starts to go
up, then suddenly people that aren't
maybe driving or impacted, well, prices
of everything go up, and so then they
ask for higher wages, and that just
leads to a stagflationary period. And
that's what we saw in the 1970s, and the
only way to really crush stagflation was
to dramatically increase interest rates
and basically crush the economy. And so,
if you're Europe, you want to really
avoid getting in a stagflationary trap.
So, anything to reduce inflation, and
what can reduce inflation? Well, not
consuming natural gas and oil.
And lo and behold, unlike in the 1970s,
there are, you know, electric vehicles,
there are heat pumps, there are ways to
begin to crush demand. And what we saw,
and you know, the debate about this is
just really bizarre.
Everyone just thinks that you
immediately have to turn to coal. And I
think in some ways we're going to see a
resurgence in coal as we saw in 2022,
but that's immediately dropped off. What
we actually saw was a massive increase
in Europe in the deployment of
renewables. At the beginning of the war
in 2022, Europe's energy generation, the
share from different mixes of sources,
fossil fuels were 40% of Europe's energy
generation in 2022, renewables were 20%.
And where they are now is renewables
have overtaken fossils. So, renewables
are now 30% and fossils at 29. There was
a real uptick, especially in the first
few years of the war. And that has left
actually Europe in a much better
position to cope with this energy
crisis. And in fact, you could also say,
from a policy perspective, Europe is
probably the most prepared around the
world to deal with such an energy crisis
because they already dealt with it. They
dealt with one four years ago. So, in
the lifespan of these policymakers. And
so, what does Europe need to do? I think
more of what it was doing in the first
few years in aftermath of the war. And
that requires some short-term subsidies
to German chemical companies and other
things like that. But, you don't want
these companies to die. But, really,
what they need to do is accelerate the
energy transition, and that could also
mean nuclear. The problem is it takes a
long time for nuclear power plants to be
built. If you can expedite that, you
don't necessarily want to cut corners
there when it comes to permitting. Maybe
you do. I don't know. Maybe there's ways
to shorten the time frame. But, you know
you can buy a lot of cheap solar panels
and deploy them fairly quickly. You
know, your car companies can produce
EVs. You know, there needs to be a
little bit of a can-do attitude here,
and not viewing it as we just got to get
to May and then everything is going to
be resolved because I think those
countries and regions that take a
slightly longer-term approach here, that
this is going to be a year-long crisis,
if not potentially longer, or at least
it's going to be sticky in terms of
getting out of this crisis, I think
we'll be much better off in the medium
term.
Another collateral
damage of this whole thing has been the
intra-NATO
relationship.
President Trump recently called NATO a
paper tiger,
and there's been a lot of tension
because Spain, for example, has closed
its airspace and bases to US planes.
Italy didn't want to let US planes that
were involved in offensive operations
use the airbase Sigonella.
France denied overflight for weapon
shipment to Israel, etc., etc. So, all
of this keeps escalating. Obviously,
Trump often sees these things as pretty
transactional, and he thinks it's
a boost for everyone with they're doing
in Iran, and doesn't understand why NATO
countries in Europe would not help. So,
that's creating a severe pain point. Not
that things were peachy before,
obviously, but things seem to be getting
worse really fast, and more damage is
happening. And I'm curious if you feel
like there's some comparisons here
2003 type tensions, or if we're even
worse than that. Oh, I think it's much
worse than 2003 in many respects.
In part because there was at least, you
know, a bunch of half of Europe, or a
lot of Europe, did support the US effort
in Iraq. I'm not saying that side was
right about the discussion, but in this
case, without telling anyone that we
were doing it, without engaging our NATO
allies and partners, and even asking
them about whether they wanted to
participate or talking with them. And
now it's sort of our sort of scapegoat
of saying, "Why don't you just open the
strait? You know, we've done all the
hard work for you. You know, we're not
going to send our navy anywhere close to
the strait because we know we'll be
could be sunk." So
>> We should say it's also ironic that this
is worse than before because from the
Secretary General's report two weeks ago
in 2025 all the allies reached 2% of GDP
on defense for first time since the 2014
commitment. So it's kind of this
split-screen image that we're seeing.
Yeah, you know, when you're the drunk
guy at the bar and you want to fight
someone and NATO's sort of sitting over
there in the corner. I mean, that's it's
out of nowhere, but it made it into
Trump's presidential address that he
gave to the country where he blamed
Europe for not siding with the US. We're
seeing some on the kind of far right
influencer side really blasting NATO for

that is being ramped up again, very much
like the freedom fries from the Iraq
days. There's a little bit less venom

very unified in going to war with Iraq.
It's very disunified when it comes to
this war. But I think this is going to
be a major source of tension. I don't
know what happens with the NATO summit
in Turkey this summer. Does that happen?
But you know, when the Trump
administration came to office I wrote a
piece about the coming collisions in
transatlantic relations. And the basic
argument was that like everything is a
potential collision point and this is
the latest one. You know, six weeks ago
we were talking about Greenland. Now
it's Iran in the strait.
You know, it could be something else in
another week or so. And I think this is
why it's increasingly becoming important
for Europe to think about having a
common foreign security policy. In the
Maastricht Treaty that was agreed to in
the early '90s they created the hope
that there would be a common foreign
security policy. What they effectively
did is just say that there would be
basically this multilateral organization
appended to the European Union that
would so to speak have a common foreign
security policy. Meaning that there was
no way of actually the EU having one
unless there's unanimity between all the
countries agreeing. And if you get
everyone to sort of agree on the same
statement well, that's a pretty blah
statement and it's not going to say very
much. And there's have been a push by
Germany and the German foreign minister
to move away from unanimity on EU
foreign policy in this term of the
commission which ends in 2029. And I
think we could see a push after the
Hungarian election
to say, "Okay, how are we doing foreign
policy in Europe? Wouldn't it be better
if we could actually just move forward
on things and not everyone has to agree
and it can be like other pieces of other
forms of legislation." This is obviously
going to be very difficult for a lot of
countries, particularly the smaller
countries. But look, if you're Estonian
you want to have a solid Russia policy
and everything is getting stuck because
there's one random election that goes
the wrong way, you know, and maybe
that's in Slovenia with 2.2 million
people and they elect a far right guy
that's kind of crazy about certain
topic. Maybe it's a far left person in
another election. You know, you can't
run a foreign policy that way where at
every corner there's an election that
could upend the ability for Europe to
speak with one voice. And if you want to
speak with one voice consistently on the
world stage
you got to get rid of unanimity and I
think this is a smart push by the
Germans and I think this is about
countries you know, do you want to hang
together or do you want to hang
separately? Do you want the European
Union to be able to speak with one voice
and be a powerful actor on the world
stage or not? Because it's simply not
going to be and it's not going to have
any presence on Middle East policy
unless it can speak with one voice. We
already talked about von der Leyen
getting getting all this crap for
calling Gulf leaders in the wake of the
attacks, but like what is supposed to
happen in Europe when it comes to
foreign policy unless you get rid of QMV
and this is I think something that we'll
see a lot more of potentially after the
Hungarian election. Yeah, probably
definitely the conversation's going to
pick up, but as you said, I think
there's going to be several member
states who will want to talk about this
in the opposite way and say, "We are not
doing this. Now is not the time."
And you could make an argument, I'm not
doing the work for them, but that
democratic representation is
having to agree on all these things even
after one random election goes another
[clears throat] way.
But the big election that we're all
looking at, which might seem random to
some people, but we've all been staring
at for a while and will be staring at
over Sunday, April 12th, obviously is in
Hungary.
Things continue to be really interesting
over there, not just because the Vice
President of the United States is
visiting Budapest as we are recording
this, but also over the weekend we heard
from Serbian authorities that they found
an explosive device near pipeline that's
close or by a pipeline that's close to
the Hungarian border. Obviously some
figures of the Orbán government quickly
ran to say maybe this was Ukraine.
Serbian authorities actually say
actually it's not. So there's there's
still a lot going on, but I think it's
really important to highlight that the
Vice President is there a few days

nothing. He obviously is saying that
it's not just a campaign for Orbán, but
just to show their support, the
closeness between the United States and
Hungary. It's the American-Hungarian Day

at a time where almost every day there
articles coming out about Orbán's links

dynamic where Vice President Vance is

towards the United States' vision for
Europe and supports its policy at the

things that are actually quite against
American interests. Yeah, I mean, we're
directly interfering
or involving ourselves in a political
election in another country
to try to sway the outcome
in a way that I can't really remember
happening in Europe. And you could point

of David Cameron before the Brexit
referendum as an example of that. And I
think the White House later regretted
that, but it was at Cameron's request
and I guess this is at Orbán's request.
But in this case like we are taking the
side of Orbán who is clearly being
helped by the Russians where his
government is clearly in cahoots with
the Russians, has been sharing
information. Budapest has become a
center for Russian espionage. It's their
kind of way into the European Union.
Undermining Ukraine and you know, right
now Hungary is stopping the EU from
funding Ukraine, right? Like that is
what they're doing. And okay, you don't
like Ukraine, but we're not funding
Ukraine. So does Vance just want Ukraine
to have no money? To just be completely
cut off? Why doesn't he ask Hungary to
lift its veto? And what this really
shows is that we're not on the side of
democracy either in Ukraine or in
Hungary, I would say. Because it is
clear that Hungary has
become an electoral autocracy. I think
it's probably an overstatement to say
it's not a democracy. It's having
elections, but the whole system is
clearly rigged in favor of the ruling
party. And this has been demonstrated in
election after election and lots of
research and studies. Anyway, where we
are is that Orbán looks set to lose this
election and potentially lose it badly.
Here you have JD Vance coming to, you
know, back Hungary and back Orbán. And
in doing so, I think he's likely going
to have real egg on his face for coming
in intervening. And all the Hungarian
pollsters say that, you know, Trump is
not popular, Vance is not popular. Peter
Magyar, the opposition leader, has
called this direct election
interference. And so I don't think this
is going to work. Instead, what it does
is it makes us incredibly anti-EU,
anti-European,
European in the air quotes of supporting
the European project. Jacob Helberg, the
undersecretary for the economic affairs,
also went to Brussels last week and just
gave a speech that was basically just
like trashing the EU but then saying
that we love the EU. I don't know, maybe
the kids call this negging or whatever
that we're going to we talk so much crap
about you, but we actually like you. It
doesn't work. Like, you know, could you
imagine a European leader coming to
America and starting a conversation and
saying, "Yeah, you're all fat and you
die early and you have so many guns."
And I mean, this is what we're doing in
Europe. It's incredibly offensive. And
meanwhile, the Hungarians, if the EU was
so bad, they have a way out.
Like they could leave.
But there's a reason why they don't do
that. One is Brussels provides them a

that money. The second thing is that the
Hungarians don't want to leave the
European Union. That would be incredibly

ruinous. And Hungary is now one of the
most corrupt, one of the poorest,
countries in Europe, where its economy

that's the model of success for the rest

the US is doing right now, and really
putting the United States on the side of
our adversary in Russia, a Trojan horse

Union that is undermining EU support for
Ukraine. And we have told
the Europeans, "Take charge of Ukraine.
That's your problem."
And then, here's this Trojan horse that

realistically, this US administration

when we talk about collisions in coming

if Orban tries to steal it or or refuses

>> I'm delighted to have Federico Steinberg

University. He's also a Senior Fellow

Federico, thanks so much for coming back

the Union, and the lack of a clear

higher, and growth is going to slow

basically demographic pressures, the

Yet,

both
address both of these at the same time

as well as addressing energy security?

European Union,

you know, energy to be relatively cheap,

This is going to be more expensive or

pan-European programs to accelerate the

seen
you know, that there's a discussion
